learn.hook: A cricket team works because the bowler, keeper and batters each do one job well. Your body runs on the same idea: division of labour.
points: In multicellular animals, similar cells with their intercellular material form tissues that perform a common function.
Animals have four basic tissue types: epithelial (covering and lining), connective (linking and supporting), muscular (movement) and neural (control and coordination).

Tissues are organised in specific proportions and patterns to form organs such as the stomach, lungs, heart and kidney. Organs working together form organ systems, such as the digestive and respiratory systems.
Division of labour among cells, tissues, organs and organ systems helps the whole body survive. The complexity of organs and organ systems shows a discernible evolutionary trend.
Morphology studies the externally visible form and features; in animals, anatomy refers to the study of the morphology of internal organs.

example.q: Arrange from simplest to most complex: organ system, cell, organ, tissue.
steps: The cell is the basic unit.
Organs work together as an organ system.

learn.reallife: At AIIMS, different departments (cardiology, nephrology, pulmonology) mirror organ systems: each specialises, and the hospital works only when all cooperate.

quiz.explain: Anatomy deals with internal organs; morphology with external form.

quiz.explain: Specialisation of parts allows efficient functioning.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all cells are identical in function
options: All cells do every job equally

quiz.explain: For example, the digestive system.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Complexity does show an evolutionary trend (A true), but animals differ in their organ systems, so R is false.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all animals are built alike

teach.praise: Chirp! Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, organs make systems. Teamwork!
teach.nudge: Good! What comes after tissues, and why is division of labour useful?

topics.title: The frog: habits and external features

learn.hook: When the monsoon arrives, frogs suddenly croak everywhere. Where were they all summer? Sleeping underground.
points: The common Indian frog is Rana tigrina (class Amphibia, phylum Chordata). Frogs are poikilotherms: their body temperature changes with the surroundings. They change colour to hide from enemies (camouflage); this protective colouration is called mimicry.
In peak summer and winter, frogs shelter in deep burrows: summer sleep is aestivation and winter sleep is hibernation.

Skin is smooth, slippery with mucus, and always moist. The dorsal side is olive green with dark irregular spots; the ventral side is uniformly pale yellow. A frog never drinks water; it absorbs water through its skin.

Body is divided into head and trunk; there is no neck or tail. A pair of nostrils lies above the mouth; bulging eyes are covered by a nictitating membrane that protects them in water; a membranous tympanum (ear) on each side receives sound.

Forelimbs end in four digits; hind limbs are larger and more muscular and end in five webbed digits for swimming. Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of each forelimb, absent in females (sexual dimorphism).

example.q: How can you tell a male frog from a female by external features?
steps: Look for sound-producing vocal sacs: present only in males.
Check the first digit of the forelimb for a copulatory pad: present only in males.
example.answer: Males have vocal sacs and copulatory pads on the forelimbs.

learn.reallife: Frogs vanish from Indian fields in the dry summer and reappear with the first monsoon showers, after aestivating in moist burrows. (Dissection of frogs has been discontinued in many Indian institutions; models, charts and virtual dissections are used instead, and wild frogs should never be harmed.)

learn.hook: A frog can breathe through its skin while sitting at the bottom of a pond. Humans cannot: we depend entirely on our lungs.
points: The body cavity holds the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, excretory and reproductive systems.
Digestive system: the alimentary canal is short because frogs are carnivores. Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → cloaca. Food is caught by a bilobed tongue.

Stomach walls secrete HCl and gastric juices; partly digested food (chyme) passes to the duodenum, which receives bile (from liver via gall bladder) and pancreatic juice through a common bile duct. Bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Villi and microvilli in the intestine absorb digested food.

Respiration in water: through the skin by diffusion (cutaneous respiration). On land: buccal cavity, skin and lungs (pulmonary respiration through elongated pink sac-like lungs in the thorax). During aestivation and hibernation, gas exchange is through the skin.
Adaptations to amphibious life: moist skin for breathing, webbed hind feet for swimming, nictitating membrane for eyes, lungs for air, and the ability to aestivate or hibernate.

example.q: Order the path of food in a frog from mouth to exit.
example.answer: Mouth, buccal cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, intestine, rectum, cloaca

learn.reallife: Frogs in paddy fields of Assam and Bengal stay submerged for long periods, relying on cutaneous respiration through their moist skin.

learn.hook: A frog's heart has three chambers, but its red blood cells keep their nuclei, unlike ours. Small differences, big stories.
points: Circulation is closed, with a well-developed lymphatic system (lymph, lymph channels, lymph nodes). The heart is in the upper body cavity, covered by the pericardium, with three chambers: two atria and one ventricle.
The sinus venosus, a triangular structure, joins the right atrium and receives blood through the venae cavae. The ventricle opens into the sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side.
Arteries carry blood from the heart; veins bring it back. Special venous connections: hepatic portal system (between intestine and liver) and renal portal system (between lower body and kidney).
Blood has plasma and cells: RBCs (erythrocytes) that are nucleated and have haemoglobin, WBCs (leucocytes) and platelets. Lymph lacks some proteins and RBCs.

Excretory system: a pair of compact, dark red, bean-like kidneys made of uriniferous tubules (nephrons), ureters, cloaca and a thin-walled urinary bladder. In males the ureters act as urinogenital ducts; in females ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca. Frogs excrete urea, so they are ureotelic.

example.q: Trace the path of blood entering a frog's heart from the body.
steps: Body blood returns through the venae cavae.
The sinus venosus joins the right atrium.
From the atria blood goes to the single ventricle, then into the conus arteriosus.
example.answer: Venae cavae → sinus venosus → right atrium → ventricle → conus arteriosus

learn.reallife: Doctors in India explain portal circulation to medical students using the human hepatic portal system; the frog shows both hepatic and renal portal systems.

topics.title: Frog control, coordination and sense organs

learn.hook: A frog's brain is tiny, but it still has three parts and ten pairs of cranial nerves, enough to snap a fly mid-air.
points: Control and coordination use both the neural system and endocrine glands. Endocrine glands of the frog: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads.
Nervous system: central (brain and spinal cord), peripheral (cranial and spinal nerves) and autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic). Ten pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain.

The brain, in a bony brain box (cranium), has fore-brain (olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon), mid-brain (pair of optic lobes) and hind-brain (cerebellum and medulla oblongata).
The medulla oblongata passes out through the foramen magnum and continues as the spinal cord inside the vertebral column.

Sense organs: touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes) and hearing (tympanum with internal ears). Eyes and internal ears are well organised; the others are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. Frog eyes are simple; the ear is for hearing and balance; there is no external ear.

example.q: Name the parts of the frog's hind-brain and the opening through which it continues as the spinal cord.
steps: The medulla passes out through the foramen magnum.
example.answer: Cerebellum and medulla oblongata; foramen magnum.

learn.reallife: Frogs in Indian fields are early warning signs of pollution: their thin skin and sensitive nervous and endocrine systems are easily affected by pesticides.

learn.hook: One female frog can lay up to 3000 eggs at a time. From each, a tadpole may swim out and transform into a frog.
points: Male organs: a pair of yellowish, ovoid testes attached to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum (mesorchium). 10 to 12 vasa efferentia enter the kidneys and open into Bidder's canal, which joins the urinogenital duct opening into the cloaca.
The cloaca is a small median chamber that passes faecal matter, urine and sperms to the exterior.
Female organs: a pair of ovaries near the kidneys with no functional connection to them; a pair of oviducts opens separately into the cloaca. A mature female lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time.
Fertilisation is external, in water. Development includes a larval stage, the tadpole, which undergoes metamorphosis into the adult.
Usefulness: frogs eat insects and protect crops; they keep ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs; in some countries frog legs are eaten.

example.q: Trace the path of sperms from the testis to the outside in a male frog.
steps: Vasa efferentia enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal.
Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca → outside.
example.answer: Testis → vasa efferentia → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca

learn.reallife: Farmers benefit from frogs in rice fields because they eat crop pests; declining frog numbers can mean more pest attacks.
